questions.q: Why does a component's `.css` file not leak its styles into other components?
options: Because of a required naming convention developers must manually follow
Because of shadow DOM -- a component's styles are automatically scoped to its own template, with no extra configuration needed
Because CSS files cannot be used in LWC at all; only inline styles are supported
Because every CSS selector must be prefixed with the component's name
questions.explain: Shadow DOM automatically scopes a component's CSS to its own template -- this happens with no naming convention, build step, or configuration required, unlike CSS-module patterns in some other frameworks.

questions.q: What does the `:host` selector target inside a component's own CSS file?
options: Every element inside the component's template
The component's own custom-element tag itself, as it sits in its parent's layout
Only elements with the class name 'host'
The parent component's root element
questions.explain: :host is a special selector that reaches the component's own custom-element tag from inside its own stylesheet -- something no normal selector targeting template content can do.

questions.q: Why are CSS custom properties (like `--badge-color`) specifically useful for theming across component boundaries?
options: They are a documented exception that inherits down through shadow DOM, letting a parent influence a child's styling without breaking encapsulation
They are the only CSS feature that works inside LWC templates at all
They automatically become @api properties on the child component
They replace the need for a component's own .css file entirely
questions.explain: Unlike most styling, which shadow DOM blocks from crossing component boundaries, CSS custom properties do inherit through shadow DOM -- making them the sanctioned mechanism for a parent to influence a child's look without the child exposing a new @api property.

questions.q: Why does Salesforce advise against writing a selector like `.slds-input { ... }` to style inside a `lightning-input` component from outside it?
options: Because .slds-input is not a real CSS class used by any base component

Because that targets a class name the developer doesn't own -- a base component's internal structure can change in a future release with no warning, since it was never part of its documented public contract
Because SLDS classes can only be used inside a component's own .css file, never from a parent
Because lightning-input does not support any CSS styling
questions.explain: Base components' internal markup and class names are implementation details, not a documented contract -- targeting them directly risks breaking silently on a future platform release.

questions.q: What should a developer do if a base component doesn't expose a styling hook they need through its own documented attributes?
options: Reach past the shadow boundary and target the base component's internal classes anyway
Build a wrapper or use a different component, rather than styling classes they don't own
File a defect, since every base component must expose every possible styling hook
Disable shadow DOM for that component entirely
questions.explain: The documented guidance is to treat a missing styling hook as a sign to use a different approach -- a wrapper component or a different base component -- rather than reaching past encapsulation to style internals you don't own.
